title: Care for and maintain electrical components of agricultural equipment

lessons.title: Basic electrics on farm machines
lessons.html:
The electrical system

Tractors, bakkies and harvesters mostly use a 12 volt system. Some big machines use 24 volts. The main parts are:

  • Battery – stores power to start the engine.
  • Starter motor – turns the engine to start it.
  • Alternator – charges the battery when the engine runs.
  • Fuses and relays – fuses protect wires from burning; relays switch big currents.
  • Wiring loom – the bundle of wires that connects everything.
  • Lights, gauges, warning lights, horn and switches.
  • Sensors – on newer tractors, for speed, temperature and the hitch.

Electricity flows from the battery positive (+), through a fuse and switch, to the part, then back to the battery negative (-) through the metal frame. This return is called the earth. A bad earth is one of the most common faults.

Safety with batteries and electrics

  • Batteries make hydrogen gas that can explode. No sparks, flames or smoking near a battery.
  • Battery acid burns skin and eyes. Wear gloves and safety glasses. If acid gets in your eyes, rinse with clean water for a long time and get medical help.
  • When you disconnect, take off the negative (-) first. When you connect, put the negative on last. This stops sparks if a spanner touches the frame.
  • Take off rings and watches. A short circuit can make a ring red hot.
  • Never replace a fuse with a bigger one or with wire. This can start a fire.

lessons.title: Caring for the battery, starter and charging system
lessons.html:
Battery care

  1. Keep the battery clean and dry. Dirt and moisture on top let power leak away.
  2. Clean white or green corrosion off the terminals with a wire brush and a mix of bicarbonate of soda and water. Rinse and dry.
  3. Put a thin layer of petroleum jelly or terminal grease on the terminals.
  4. Check the clamps are tight and the battery is held down firmly.
  5. On batteries with caps, check the fluid level covers the plates. Top up with distilled water only, never acid or tap water.
  6. Check the voltage with a multimeter. A fully charged 12 volt battery reads about 12.6 volts with the engine off.

Charging and jump starting

  • Charge in a place with fresh air, away from sparks.
  • Switch the charger off before connecting or disconnecting the clamps.
  • When jump starting, connect positive to positive, then the negative lead to a metal part of the engine of the flat machine, away from the battery. Follow the machine manual – some modern tractors have special jump points.
  • Never jump start a frozen or damaged battery.

Starter and alternator

  • Check the fan belt that drives the alternator for cracks and tension.
  • With the engine running, the battery voltage should be higher than with the engine off. If not, the alternator may not be charging. Report it.
  • Check the thick starter cables for damage and tight connections.
  • Do not crank the starter for long periods. Let it rest between tries so it does not overheat.

lessons.title: Wiring, lights and finding simple faults
lessons.html:
Looking after wiring

Farm machines work in dust, mud, water and vibration. Wires get damaged easily. Check them regularly:

  • Look for wires rubbing on sharp metal, hot exhausts or moving parts.
  • Look for cracked insulation and green corrosion in plugs.
  • Check rats have not chewed wires, especially on machines parked in sheds over winter.
  • Keep wires tied with cable ties and away from heat.
  • Clean plugs with contact cleaner. Do not pressure-wash electrical parts directly.

Lights

Working lights are needed for safety, especially on the road and for night work in harvest. Check headlights, tail lights, brake lights, indicators and the rotating beacon. Replace blown bulbs with the same type and watt rating. Clean the lenses.

Finding simple faults with a multimeter

  1. Check the fuse first. Replace a blown fuse with the same rating. If it blows again, there is a short circuit – report it.
  2. Set the multimeter to DC volts. Put the black lead on a good earth and the red lead at the part. With the switch on, you should read close to battery voltage.
  3. If there is voltage but the part does not work, check the earth wire.
  4. If there is no voltage, follow the wire back to find the break.

Write all faults and work done on the job card.

Key points

  • Disconnect the negative first and connect it last.
  • Keep battery terminals clean, tight and greased; top up with distilled water only.
  • Never fit a bigger fuse or a wire in place of a fuse.
  • Check wiring for rubbing, heat damage and rats.
  • Use a multimeter to check fuses, voltage and earths.
